scope: Independent technical-source audit of language, inheritance, interface-storage, and default-interface implementation claims in frozen B09v1. Not semantic/cross-unit package acceptance, producer validation, or runtime acceptance.

references.supports: Interfaces define contracts/capabilities; classes may implement multiple interfaces, while a class has one direct base class; interfaces do not provide instance storage.
Abstract/virtual base-class behavior, derived-class overrides, and the distinction between class inheritance and interface implementation.
Interface member bodies and the rule that interfaces cannot contain instance fields or instance auto-properties requiring hidden instance state.
Default interface implementations can add a member body and allow implementers to provide a more specific implementation.
CS8701 identifies target-runtime support as a separate requirement from language version; default interface implementation requires .NET Core 3.0 or .NET 5+.

items.finding: The unrelated bundle types share a pricing contract but no common state or implementation; a capability interface is technically appropriate. The prompt stipulates the per-bundle rule, so no global default is inferred.
A base class may hold shared instance state and a common sequence with a virtual/protected variation point. The interface-default alternative does not replace the stated shared base state/workflow.
C# classes have one direct base class but can implement multiple interfaces; a narrow interface lets both SDK-derived assets preserve their existing bases while exposing the common operation.

The abstract base can hold common instance fields and validation implementation while both concrete approvals continue to be consumed through IUsageApproval. The alternatives claiming that an interface provides shared instance storage are false.
An adapter-backed interface can expose one request-scoped operation across unrelated vendor hierarchies; the prompt explicitly rules out shared mutable state and a context-free cached answer.

The stem explicitly states that older client runtimes lack default-interface-implementation support and no safe default can authorize disclosure. An opt-in capability interface avoids requiring the old implementation to implement the new operation or pretending an unsupported runtime can execute it.
An interface returning the two stored identifiers expresses the narrow caller contract across unrelated implementations; the prompt explicitly excludes shared playback state.

The described controlled family shares instance data and algorithm order, so an abstract base with one predicate hook is technically coherent. This is a design fit judgment based on the scenario's stated facts, not a universal rule that all such algorithms require inheritance.
A narrow interface can bridge unrelated SDK base types and expose stable segment IDs without requiring the editor to know provider metadata or storage representation.
The implementation family can retain shared instance lifecycle state in an abstract base while callers continue to depend on ITemporaryRole. Interfaces do not supply common instance fields.

The prompt states that only some providers implement the optional operation and no correct default can be computed. A separate capability interface makes support explicit without adding a required member to the released interface.
Provider adapters can map distinct SDK request types to a shared billing operation/result contract; the prompt states there is no shared base state to reuse.

The existing abstract base owns the shared immutable ordering value and behavior; keeping that rule on the shared base is consistent with C# inheritance. Scenario guarantees about EffectiveAt are stipulated facts.
A base class can own the shared committed-window state and invariant workflow while a virtual/protected hook varies the reading source. The scenario supplies this controlled-family guarantee.

C# 8 or later establishes language-version support for default interface member syntax, but does not establish that each target runtime supports executing default interface implementations. Microsoft documents CS8701 when the target runtime lacks support and lists .NET Core 3.0 / .NET 5+ as the runtime minimum. The prompt omits target-runtime support, so the keyed design is not established for every stated consumer.
items.smallestCorrection: State that all target runtimes support default interface implementations (in addition to the C# language-version premise), or use a separately implemented capability/adapter that does not require this runtime feature.
items.secondarySingleAnswerNote: The stem also does not explicitly require existing provider implementations to remain unchanged; if that compatibility objective is needed to distinguish a default body from adding an abstract member, state it. The source-backed target-runtime omission is the primary blocker.

items.finding: A small interface expresses the common ID and request-scoped eligibility capability without forcing unrelated HR models into one class hierarchy or adding provider-specific profile fields.

The controlled base can own coordinates, conflicts, and the stable merge sequence, leaving the explicitly identified comparison variation as a hook. This depends on scenario-provided invariants, not a general C# guarantee.

The private shared component state and total sequence belong to the described implementation base; the public interface can remain the consumer-facing contract. A default interface body cannot directly read the base class's private instance fields.

limitations: No C# compiler was available (`dotnet`, `csc`, and `mcs` were absent), so no compiler probe was run. Findings use official Microsoft documentation and inspection of the frozen whole objects.
Scenario-specific policy and behavior statements are treated as explicit fictional premises, not generalized language/API guarantees.
This audit does not establish whole-package semantic acceptance, source activation, or actual consumer runtime support.
